threat.notes: extent = share of the eventual peak-to-trough fall in the monthly-average S&P 500 (peak Oct 2007 avg 1539.66, trough Mar 2009 avg 757.13, a 51% fall), plotted at mid-month. A market-value proxy for how far the contagion had spread through the financial system; not a count of people. Note the shape: ~18 months of slow drift to 0.41, then 0.41 -> 0.73 in one month after Lehman (Sep 15 2008, t=403). Daily closes would show a sharper crash; monthly averages smooth it.

aggregation.notes: Derived from documented response dates (days after Aug 9 2007), not a measured distribution: p10 = first coordinated central-bank liquidity (TAF, Dec 12 2007), median = coordinated global rate cut and bank recapitalisations (Oct 8 2008, 23 days after Lehman), p90 = structural reform law (Jul 21 2010). Dates other than TAF and t0 are well-established but were not seen verbatim in a snippet this pass; confirm against s4/s5 before on-screen use.

deploy.notes: Proxy: days from the Oct 8 2008 coordinated response to the market's monthly-average trough (Mar 2009; daily low Mar 9 2009). Timing only; this does not establish causation.

ai_counterfactual.basis: Illustrative. The missing fragment was a shared map of who was exposed to whom; the pieces sat in separate institutions' books. Assembling exposure data across institutions is document-heavy expert work of the kind inside the ~17.4 h 50% task horizon in RATES.md (METR entry) per institution, and RATES.md's ~40x/year fall in AI cost at fixed capability makes running it across thousands of books cheap. Assumed: the Oct 2008 coordinated response is assembled at the first large failure (Bear Stearns, day 220) instead of day 426. Political decisions (e.g. passing a rescue law) still take human time, and the counterfactual does not assume the crisis is avoided.
ai_counterfactual.label: illustrative

gap_summary: The last 59% of the market fall happened in ~6 months after Lehman, with 32% of it in a single month; the coordinated response took 426 days from the first freeze, and structural reform 1,077.
